front.title: Accountability Between Administrative Domains in Delay-Tolerant Networks

abstract.t: As bundles cross Administrative Domains run by different agencies and companies, each domain can show only its own logs of what it carried. This document describes how work already before the DTN Working Group fits together to give portable, independently verifiable evidence of inter-domain carriage: the DTN Peering Protocol for routes and domain identity, the Traceroute Extension Block for path diagnostics, signed custody receipts for evidence of holding, the Secure Bundle Audit Mechanism for dropped security operations, and the BPSec COSE context. It proposes a small number of connections between them, all optional and none requiring a change to the Bundle Protocol: endorsing custodian keys with a domain's peering key, advertising a domain's receipt policy with its routes, checking a route's domain path against the custody evidence, an optional signature for traceroute hop-records, and sizing unsigned stretches with the Hop Count.

note.name: About This Document
note.t:
This is a framework for discussion. A reference implementation of the custody receipts and of the signed hop-record profile is at

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The DTN Peering Protocol describes the Solar System DTN as a set of Administrative Domains: space agencies, commercial operators and research networks that advertise reachability to one another. Its own scenarios include a commercial operator advertising transit capacity to a government science network, and two agencies' networks exchanging traffic.

Every one of those relationships raises the same questions after the fact. Did the other domain carry the bundle? When did it hold it? Which domains did a bundle actually cross, and did that match the route that was advertised? Today the answers are each domain's own logs, which another domain can only take on trust.

Several pieces of work before the DTN Working Group each address part of this. This document does not define a new protocol. It describes how those pieces fit, states the requirements they meet together, and proposes the connections that are missing.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
Administrative Domain (AD), DPP speaker and AD identity are used as in . Custodian and custody receipt are used as in . Hop-record is used as in .

ol.li: Evidence is portable: a third party can verify it, later and offline, without contacting the domains that produced it.
Participation is optional per node and per domain; nodes that do not take part forward bundles as they do today.
No change to the Bundle Protocol or to BPSec is needed.
Missing evidence is reported as missing and never inferred.
Evidence is bound to a specific bundle and the payload bytes held, so it cannot be moved to another bundle.
Keys used for evidence chain to an identity the domains already verify for routing.

section.name: The Building Blocks
section.t: The work considered here is the DTN Peering Protocol , the Traceroute Extension Block , the Custody Receipt Block , the Secure Bundle Audit Mechanism , Bundle-in-Bundle Encapsulation and CCSDS custody transfer , and the BPSec COSE context .

section.name: Custodian Keys Endorsed by the Domain's Peering Key
section.t: The custody receipt draft leaves key distribution out of scope. DPP already gives every AD an Ed25519 key published in DNS at _dtn_domain.<AD-Domain> and verified by peers in a challenge-response handshake. The same algorithm and the same key encoding (DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo, base64) are used by custody receipts.

Proposal: an AD endorses each of its custodians with a small COSE_Sign1 by its DPP key over the custodian's node ID, public key and validity period. A verifier that knows the AD (from the route, or from the custodian's node ID) fetches the AD key from DNS, checks the endorsement, and then checks the receipt. Only one key per AD is published in DNS; custodian keys rotate without DNS changes. How endorsements are distributed (with the bundle, over DPP, or by a published list) is an open question.

section.name: Receipt Policy Advertised With Routes
section.t: DPP advertisements carry extensible attributes. Proposal: an optional attribute stating an AD's receipt policy for the routes it advertises: none, offered (its custodians sign when the block is present), or required (it will only carry bundles under a receipt agreement). Peers can then prefer routes whose evidence they will be able to check.

section.name: Checking a Route's Domain Path Against the Evidence
section.t: A DPP route carries ad_path, the list of ADs it traverses. Once a bundle is delivered, the ADs of its endorsed custodians can be compared with the ad_path of the route that was used. A domain on the path with no receipt is a gap in the evidence; a receipt from a domain not on the path shows the bundle left the advertised route. Both are reported, neither is inferred.

section.name: An Optional Signature for Traceroute Hop-Records
section.t: The Traceroute Extension Block and the Custody Receipt Block record nearly the same facts per hop: the node, the node it received from, and a time. TREB's records are, by its own security section, unauthenticated and diagnostic only.

Proposal: an optional eighth element in a TREB hop-record, a COSE_Sign1 by the recording node with a detached payload (the CBOR encoding of the seven existing fields) and external additional authenticated data of the bundle identity and the SHA-256 of the payload block's data. A reader that ignores the eighth element sees an unchanged TREB hop-record; a verifier with the node's key gets custody-grade evidence. A shared hop-record shape lets diagnostics and accountability use one structure where both are wanted.

section.name: Sizing Unsigned Stretches
section.t: Both drafts observe that the Previous Node block names only the last node of an unsigned stretch. TREB already uses the Hop Count block to count the hops made by transparent nodes. Recording the Hop Count value in each custody receipt does the same for receipts, so a verifier can say how many unsigned hops lie between two signed ones.

section.name: Per-Hop Block Lifecycle
section.t: Blocks that nodes change in transit lose end-to-end BPSec protection by construction. The receipt block and signed hop-records follow a third pattern: entries are appended, never changed, and each is signed by the node that added it, so earlier entries stay verifiable end to end without any BPSec operation outliving a hop. Such blocks should not be targets of a BIB or BCB. This is offered as input to the group's discussion of per-hop blocks.

section.name: Settlement
section.t: How domains price or settle carriage is out of scope. This framework only ensures that bilateral agreements can refer to evidence both parties, and a third party, can check. For high volumes, a custodian can sign one receipt per contact over a Merkle root of the bundles it held, with inclusion proofs per bundle, as the reference implementation does.

section.name: Deployment
section.t: Each connection is independent and optional. Custody receipts are carried byte-identical today by µD3TN, NASA HDTN, JPL ION and Hardy, none of which implement them, and a payload BIB beside them still verifies. A domain can start signing receipts without any peer changing, and verifiers report every stretch it does not cover.

ul.li: Is the DTN Working Group the right home for inter-domain accountability, or only for its protocol pieces?
How should custodian endorsements be distributed?
Should the receipt policy attribute be defined in DPP or in a separate document?
Would the TREB authors welcome an optional signed hop-record, and should custody receipts adopt the TREB hop-record shape?

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The framework rests on three assumptions: AD keys published in DNS are as trustworthy as DPP requires; custodian endorsements are checked for validity periods and revocation; and verifiers never accept a key carried with the evidence itself. A compromised custodian key can sign false receipts until its endorsement expires or is revoked. Evidence can be stripped by any forwarder; stripping shows as a gap. Receipts and hop-records reveal routes and timing to anyone who can read the bundle.
